summary: Describes how the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP, RFC 4340) uses Service Codes, which identify the intended application or service when a connection is requested. They offer more flexibility than relying only on port numbers.

eli5.summary: When knocking on a door you can also say what you want. A service code is that short message telling the other side which service you wish to use.

subtitle: How a 32-bit Service Code in DCCP names the service a client wants, so port numbers no longer have to do all the work.

tldr.problem: Published port numbers are scarce and easy to collide on, and port-based firewalls push applications to disguise themselves as other applications.
tldr.mechanism: DCCP carries a 4-byte Service Code in the DCCP-Request, and the server accepts a connection only if the destination port is associated with that code. One listening port can serve several codes.
tldr.outcome: The RFC clarifies RFC 4340 and updates it. It is a Proposed Standard that was itself updated by RFC 6335.

today: RFC 5595 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4340, and it has itself been updated by RFC 6335. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Service Codes Exist
sections.content:
DCCP defines a Service Code as a 4-byte (32-bit) value that describes the application-level service a client wants to reach. It names the protocol or standard profile used above DCCP, not a variant of one. The client puts it in the DCCP-Request packet, and each application associates one or more Service Codes with each listening port.

RFC 5595 exists because RFC 4340 left out the motivation for Service Codes and did not properly describe how Well Known and Registered server ports relate to them. This document fills that gap. It also notes that Service Codes are not meant to be DCCP-specific, so other transport protocols may find a similar idea useful.

Middleboxes such as firewalls and NATs can use the code to learn the intended service more precisely than they could from the server port alone.
sections.eli5: A port is the door number. The Service Code is the sticky note that says which shop behind the door you want.

sections.title: The Problem With Published Ports
sections.content:
TCP, UDP, SCTP and UDP-Lite use Published port numbers from the Well Known or Registered ranges. Getting one means registering with IANA, and the 16-bit space is not large enough for easy, unregulated allocation. The RFC lists three coupled problems:

  • Many applications use unregistered ports and may collide with each other.
  • Port-based firewalls encourage applications to disguise themselves as others, which pushes firewall writers toward deep packet inspection.
  • ISPs often deploy transparent proxies, for example redirecting TCP requests for port 80 to a web proxy.

The DCCP designers wanted a 32-bit server port space, but that would add overhead for low-rate applications. Their answer was a 32-bit Service Code carried only in the DCCP-Request, so the data flow pays no extra cost. An early idea of identifying connections by a 32-bit identifier alone was dropped because it would prevent two servers for the same service on one machine and might hinder use through NATs. RFC 4340 kept two 16-bit ports instead.

That brought back a new problem: obtaining a unique Registered DCCP port may not stay possible. So the RFC motivates associating more than one Service Code with a listening port.
sections.eli5: There are only so many door numbers, and everyone wants one. So DCCP lets many shops share a door and tells them apart by the note each visitor carries.

sections.title: Ports and Service Code Values
sections.content:
DCCP demultiplexes packets by the four values source address, source port, destination address and destination port, as TCP does. DCCP supports Well Known and Registered ports, allocated in the DCCP IANA Port Numbers registry. Each Registered DCCP port MUST be associated with at least one pre-defined Service Code. Applications that do not need such a port SHOULD use a Dynamic port, which clients can learn from an SDP record exchanged out of band or from DNS SRV records.

A Service Code is written as a decimal number (the canonical form), a 4-character ASCII string or an 8-digit hexadecimal number. All standards-assigned codes, including those from IANA, must be representable in ASCII. Private Service Codes are not centrally allocated and use the decimal range 1056964608-1073741823.

Endpoints MUST associate a Service Code with every DCCP socket, active or passive. A single listening port may have several codes. In the packet types defined at the time, the code appears only in DCCP-Request and DCCP-Response.

Three special rules apply:

  • A code of zero means no meaningful code. Applications SHOULD NOT use it, and should pick a private code for a temporary need.
  • The value 4294967295 (0xFFFFFFFF) is invalid. Implementations MUST NOT accept a DCCP-Request carrying it.
  • New versions of an application that negotiates its own version SHOULD keep the same code.
sections.eli5: A Service Code is a four-letter nickname for a service, like a team name. Some nicknames are saved for official teams, some are free for anyone to borrow, and zero means no nickname at all.

sections.title: Hashing a Service Code to a Port
sections.content:
Applications that use neither out-of-band signalling nor an IANA-assigned port still need client and server to agree on a port. The RFC offers an optional method that derives a default server port in the Dynamic range from the Service Code, written in C as shown below. Here sc[3] is the least significant byte.

For example, the code SC:fdpz maps to server port 64634. The method tries to give different codes different ports but does not guarantee uniqueness. It keeps the 4 lowest bits of the final bytes, so many common series of codes land on adjacent ports, and it avoids port 0xFFFF, which is not accessible on all host platforms. Because DCCP servers are told apart by Service Code, another application using the same port does no harm.
sections.eli5: It is a recipe that turns a service's nickname into a door number, so both sides can guess the same door without calling each other first.

sections.title: How Clients, Networks and Servers Use the Code
sections.content:
A client issues a DCCP-Request with a Service Code and a destination port it expects to match that code. A server checks whether a matching service exists on that port. If so, it associates the session with the code and returns a DCCP-Response containing a copy of the Service Code. If not, it rejects the request with a DCCP-Reset.

When the port is not bound to any server, the host MUST reject with Reset Code "Connection Refused" (it may use "Too Busy"). When the port is bound but not associated with the code, the server SHOULD reset with Reset Code 8, "Bad Service Code".

Two servers must not claim the same code on the same port, and an implementation MUST disallow it. The RFC replaces the RFC 4340 text so that an implementation SHOULD allow more than one Service Code on a passive port, and SHOULD tell a server which code an active connection selected. A passive port may have many codes, but an active connection has exactly one.

For middleboxes, new DCCP connections are identified by server port plus Service Code in addition to the IP address. A middlebox that wants to tell applications apart SHOULD test the code as well as the port. One that does not modify the application, such as a NAT or firewall, MUST NOT change it. There is no guarantee that the traffic really matches the code, so deep packet inspection may still be used.

A host may also launch a server on demand when a DCCP-Request arrives, in a way that could resemble inetd.
sections.eli5: The visitor says which door and which shop. If the shop is not behind that door, the doorman sends them away with a note saying the shop was wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document describes usage and adds no new protocol functions. All IPsec modes protect the integrity of the DCCP header, so the Service Code cannot be changed unnoticed in the network. IPsec ESP can also encrypt the field, which hides it from middleboxes. Application-layer security such as DTLS does not protect the DCCP header.

  • Port reuse: because codes let applications share a port safely, port reuse in DCCP may be more common than in TCP and UDP.
  • Reconnaissance: a server using Service Codes immediately confirms or denies that a given service is present, which may help port scanning.
  • Mapping: the same application may be reached by several codes, for example one for use directly on DCCP and another over DTLS, so mapping a code to a service needs care.
  • Denial of service: processing codes may cost more than handling ports, so implementors need to guard against new opportunities.
  • IPsec and firewalls: IKEv2 does not currently specify a way to use Service Codes when setting up a security association. New IPsec and firewall implementations may interpret the code but should not rely on ports or codes to indicate a specific service.
sections.eli5: Because the doorman answers right away, a snoop can tell which shops are inside. And a shop can have more than one nickname, so be careful what you assume.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: RFC 5595 does not change the IANA allocation procedures for the DCCP Port Number and DCCP Service Codes registries defined in RFC 4340. It notes that an approved document such as an RFC is not required to apply for a Service Code or port number, although an RFC may be used to request values through its IANA Considerations section. A specification is required to allocate a Service Code that uses a combination of ASCII digits, uppercase letters, and the characters space, '-', '.' and '/'.
sections.eli5: Getting a nickname from the official list is easy and usually needs no paperwork, except for certain special kinds of nicknames.

messages.note: Sent if the port is associated with the code; returns a copy of the code.

messages.label: DCCP-Reset
messages.note: Sent instead if the service is not available, for example Reset Code 8, Bad Service Code.
